CHIEF COMPLAINT
Hypertension and palpitations

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Mr. Jordan Roberts is a 49-year-old male with a long-standing history of hypertension since young age presenting for evaluation. He reports a recent emergency room visit in March with elevated blood pressure and palpitations, which he attributes to consuming several cups of coffee without breakfast that day, possibly representing a panic attack. He denies recurrence of palpitations since that time. He has a strong family history of hypertension. Approximately one month ago, his new primary care doctor initiated a new antihypertensive regimen. He is currently checking his blood pressure at home daily, with morning readings ranging from 146-155 mmHg. He reports attempting to reduce his salt intake and exercises on the treadmill when able. He remains on three maxed-dose antihypertensive medications with inadequate blood pressure control.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Denies recurrent palpitations. Denies chest pain, dyspnea, or lower extremity swelling.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Hypertension (since young age)

MEDICATIONS
Benicar HCT (Olmesartan 40/Hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg)
Amlodipine 10 mg daily

ALLERGIES
Not documented

FAMILY HISTORY
Strong family history of hypertension

SOCIAL HISTORY
Lives with girlfriend. Attempts dietary salt restriction. Exercises on treadmill intermittently.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital Signs: Home blood pressure readings 146-155 mmHg
General: Alert and oriented
Cardiovascular: Heart sounds normal, no murmurs
Pulmonary: Lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender
Extremities: No ankle or foot edema

RESULTS
Potassium: 4.0 (one week ago)
Thyroid profile available from March 1, 2021

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Resistant hypertension on maximal therapy with three antihypertensive agents. Initiated spironolactone to address possible primary hyperaldosteronism. Patient counseled on potential side effects including dizziness, gynecomastia (rare, 1 in 100 men), and electrolyte disturbances. Discussed need for adequate hydration to prevent dehydration and associated symptoms. Advised on DASH diet, salt restriction (goal <2000 mg/day, ideally 1500 mg/day), and regular aerobic exercise (30 minutes most days) for blood pressure reduction. Provided education materials from American Heart Association website. Metabolic panel and blood pressure recheck scheduled in 2 weeks to monitor potassium and sodium levels. If inadequate response to spironolactone, referral to resistant hypertension clinic for evaluation of secondary causes and consideration of renal denervation procedure. Follow-up appointment in 2 weeks.
